subtopic_detail: Planning birth when ultrasound suggests abnormal placental invasion
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 34 year old woman in her fourth pregnancy at 32 weeks who has had two previous caesarean sections and one vaginal birth. She has had no bleeding, no contractions and no pain, and she attends for a routine growth and placental localisation scan.

The report describes an anterior placenta covering the internal cervical os, loss of the hypoechoic clear zone between placenta and myometrium, multiple placental lacunae with turbulent flow, and interruption of the interface between the uterine serosa and the bladder wall. Foetal growth is on the 55th centile with normal Dopplers, and she lives 40 minutes from a tertiary maternity unit.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 144 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), ferritin 42 micrograms/L (30-300), platelets 236 x10^9/L (150-400), blood group O RhD positive with no atypical antibodies
data_table.Imaging: Anterior placenta covering the internal os with loss of the clear zone, multiple lacunae with turbulent flow and bladder wall interface interruption

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for birth?

options.text: Plan caesarean hysterectomy at 34 to 36 weeks in a specialist centre
options.rationale: These ultrasound features indicate placenta accreta spectrum, and Australian practice is planned birth at 34 to 36 weeks with the placenta left in situ and hysterectomy performed by a multidisciplinary team in a centre with interventional radiology, critical care and massive transfusion capability (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum).

options.text: Plan caesarean at 39 weeks with attempted manual removal of the placenta
options.rationale: Attempting to separate an abnormally invasive placenta is the single act most likely to cause catastrophic haemorrhage, and waiting to 39 weeks greatly increases the chance of an unplanned emergency birth (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum).

options.text: Plan induction of labour at 37 weeks with continuous monitoring
options.rationale: Labour is contraindicated with a placenta covering the internal os regardless of invasion, and the near pair distinction is that praevia alone determines mode of birth while accreta spectrum determines timing and setting as well (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum).
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum

options.text: Plan caesarean at 37 weeks with uterine artery embolisation first
options.rationale: Prophylactic arterial occlusion is an adjunct used within a planned procedure rather than a substitute for planning the timing and place of birth, and its benefit remains unproven (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum).

options.text: Repeat the ultrasound at 36 weeks before making any birth plan
options.rationale: Deferring the plan wastes the interval in which corticosteroids, blood product planning and transfer to an appropriate centre must be arranged, and around a third of these women bleed before their planned date (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Accreta Spectrum).

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum is rising in incidence in step with the caesarean section rate, and the combination of a previous caesarean with an anterior placenta praevia is the highest risk situation in obstetrics. Antenatal diagnosis is what changes outcome, because planned birth in an appropriate centre halves major haemorrhage and intensive care admission compared with unexpected diagnosis at delivery. The ultrasound features to know are loss of the clear zone, placental lacunae with turbulent flow, bladder line interruption, myometrial thinning and increased subplacental vascularity, with magnetic resonance imaging reserved for posterior placentas or uncertain findings. Delivery is planned before labour begins, usually at 34 to 36 weeks after corticosteroids, with the whole team, cross matched blood and cell salvage available, and the placenta is left undisturbed while hysterectomy proceeds.
key_points: Previous caesarean with an anterior praevia is the highest risk combination
Loss of the clear zone, lacunae and bladder line interruption are the key ultrasound signs
Plan birth at 34 to 36 weeks before labour begins
Leave the placenta in situ rather than attempting removal
Deliver in a centre with interventional radiology and massive transfusion capacity
explanation.pearls: The risk of accreta spectrum in a woman with placenta praevia rises from about 3 per cent with no previous caesarean to over 40 per cent with two or more, which is why the number of previous caesareans is the first question asked when a praevia is reported.

sources.label: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and Accreta Spectrum

subtopic_detail: Choosing route and progestogen for hormone therapy when thrombotic risk is elevated
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 53 year old woman who has had no periods for 14 months and describes more than a dozen drenching hot flushes a day with night sweats that wake her three or four times. She has stopped going to her walking group because of them and says she is exhausted.

Her body mass index is 34 kg per square metre. Eight years ago she had a deep vein thrombosis in the six weeks after a knee arthroscopy, treated with six months of anticoagulation, and a thrombophilia screen at the time was negative. Her uterus is intact, her blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg, she has never smoked and her mammogram three months ago was reported as normal.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests, thyroid stimulating hormone, fasting lipids and glucose within normal limits
data_table.Screening: Mammogram three months ago reported as normal, cervical screening up to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Commence oral conjugated oestrogen with medroxyprogesterone acetate
options.rationale: Oral oestrogen undergoes first pass hepatic metabolism and raises the risk of venous thromboembolism, and medroxyprogesterone acetate carries a higher breast cancer and thrombotic signal than micronised progesterone (Source: Australasian Menopause Society).

options.text: Commence transdermal oestradiol with micronised progesterone orally
options.rationale: Transdermal oestradiol avoids first pass metabolism and has not been associated with increased venous thromboembolism, and micronised progesterone provides the endometrial protection required by an intact uterus with the most favourable risk profile (Source: Australasian Menopause Society; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence oral oestradiol 2 mg daily without a progestogen component
options.rationale: Unopposed oestrogen in a woman with an intact uterus causes endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma, and the oral route adds the thrombotic concern (Source: Australasian Menopause Society).

options.text: Commence tibolone 2.5 mg daily and review the symptoms in three months
options.rationale: Tibolone is effective for vasomotor symptoms but is associated with an increased risk of stroke in older women and does not have the thrombotic safety data of transdermal oestradiol (Source: Australasian Menopause Society).

options.text: Decline menopausal hormone therapy and commence venlafaxine instead
options.rationale: A previous provoked thrombosis with a negative thrombophilia screen is not a contraindication to transdermal therapy, and a non hormonal alternative gives roughly half the symptom reduction (Source: Australasian Menopause Society).

explanation.summary: Menopausal hormone therapy remains the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms, and the modern decision is less about whether to prescribe than about which route and which progestogen. Route matters because oral oestrogen increases hepatic production of clotting factors, roughly doubling venous thromboembolism risk, while transdermal delivery bypasses the liver and has not shown that association in observational data. Progestogen choice matters because micronised progesterone and dydrogesterone carry a lower breast cancer signal than synthetic progestogens, while providing adequate endometrial protection. A single provoked thrombosis with a negative thrombophilia screen and no ongoing risk factor does not preclude therapy, whereas unprovoked or recurrent events, or an inherited thrombophilia, warrant haematology input first. Obesity independently raises baseline thrombotic risk, which strengthens rather than removes the case for the transdermal route.
key_points: Transdermal oestradiol avoids the first pass hepatic effect on clotting factors
An intact uterus always requires a progestogen for endometrial protection
Micronised progesterone has the most favourable breast and thrombotic profile
A single provoked thrombosis is not an absolute contraindication
Obesity raises baseline thrombotic risk and favours the transdermal route
explanation.pearls: Transdermal oestradiol at doses of 50 micrograms per 24 hours or less has not been shown to increase venous thromboembolism risk even in women with a prior provoked event, which is the specific evidence that allows treatment in this situation.

subtopic_detail: Operative decision for adnexal torsion in the second trimester
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 27 year old woman at 14 weeks in her first pregnancy who developed severe right sided lower abdominal pain five hours ago while hanging out washing. The pain comes in waves and she has vomited four times.

A 7 cm simple right ovarian cyst was noted at her dating scan and she has had no bleeding. Her abdomen is tender in the right iliac fossa with guarding, and the cervix is closed on speculum examination. Ultrasound today shows an oedematous right ovary measuring 8 cm with follicles displaced to the periphery, a twisted vascular pedicle and no venous flow within the ovary, with a viable intrauterine pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 106 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 152 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 12 mg/L (less than 5), haemoglobin 116 g/L (115-155), midstream urine negative
data_table.Imaging: Enlarged oedematous right ovary with peripherally displaced follicles, twisted vascular pedicle and absent intraovarian venous flow

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Perform laparoscopic oophorectomy of the affected right ovary
options.rationale: Removing the ovary because it looks dark and oedematous is the classic error, since the appearance at surgery correlates poorly with viability and most untwisted ovaries recover function (Source: RANZCOG Adnexal Masses in Pregnancy).

options.text: Manage conservatively with analgesia and repeat ultrasound in 24 hours
options.rationale: Torsion is a surgical emergency in which every hour of delay increases the chance of irreversible infarction, and imaging in 24 hours will only document a dead ovary (Source: RANZCOG Adnexal Masses in Pregnancy).

options.text: Perform laparoscopic detorsion with conservation of the ovary
options.rationale: Prompt laparoscopic untwisting with ovarian conservation is the standard approach at any age when future fertility matters, and laparoscopy is safe in the second trimester with appropriate port placement (Source: RANZCOG Adnexal Masses in Pregnancy).

options.text: Perform laparotomy with oophorectomy and salpingectomy on the right
options.rationale: Laparotomy is reserved for suspected malignancy, haemodynamic instability or where laparoscopic access is not feasible, and it combines an unnecessary open approach with unnecessary ovarian loss (Source: RANZCOG Adnexal Masses in Pregnancy).

options.text: Defer surgery until after 16 weeks when the placenta has taken over
options.rationale: The second trimester is the preferred window for non urgent surgery in pregnancy, but this is an emergency where the timing rule does not apply (Source: RANZCOG Adnexal Masses in Pregnancy).

explanation.summary: Adnexal torsion is around five times more common in pregnancy than outside it, most often in the first and early second trimesters when an enlarged corpus luteum or a persistent cyst provides the lead point. Ultrasound findings of an enlarged oedematous ovary with peripherally displaced follicles and a twisted pedicle are more reliable than Doppler flow, because dual blood supply means arterial flow can persist in a torted ovary and its presence does not exclude the diagnosis. The historical practice of removing a blue or black ovary has been abandoned, since colour at operation reflects venous congestion rather than necrosis and the great majority of conserved ovaries regain follicular activity on later imaging. Malignancy risk in a torted ovary is low, and cystectomy at the same operation is often deferred to allow the oedema to settle. In pregnancy, laparoscopy is safe with open entry or a left upper quadrant approach and appropriate insufflation pressures.
key_points: Preserved Doppler arterial flow does not exclude ovarian torsion
Peripherally displaced follicles and a twisted pedicle are the key ultrasound signs
The colour of the ovary at surgery does not predict recovery of function
Detorsion with conservation is standard where fertility matters
Laparoscopy is safe in the second trimester with appropriate entry technique
explanation.pearls: Most conserved ovaries show normal follicular development on ultrasound within three to six months of detorsion, and the theoretical risk of thromboembolism from untwisting a congested pedicle has not been borne out in practice.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria Clinical Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Matching treatment of heavy menstrual bleeding to fibroid location when fertility is intended
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 41 year old woman with two years of periods so heavy that she soaks through a pad each hour on the worst days and passes clots the size of coins. She has been trying to conceive for eight months and has not been pregnant before.

She has no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding and no pelvic pain. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a uterus of ten week size containing a single 3 cm submucosal fibroid that indents the cavity with less than half its volume within the myometrium, an endometrium of 6 mm and normal ovaries. Her partner's semen analysis is normal and her cervical screening is up to date.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 74 fL (80-100), ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-300), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Single 3 cm submucosal fibroid indenting the endometrial cavity with less than half its volume intramural, endometrium 6 mm, ovaries normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system in the clinic
options.rationale: The intrauterine system is first line for heavy menstrual bleeding without cavity distortion, but it is contraceptive and expulsion rates are high when a submucosal fibroid distorts the cavity (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding).

options.text: Refer for uterine artery embolisation by interventional radiology
options.rationale: Embolisation is effective for bulk symptoms from intramural fibroids but is not recommended for women intending pregnancy because of effects on ovarian reserve and placentation (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding).

options.text: Prescribe tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during her periods
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid reduces blood loss by around a third and is a useful holding measure, but it does not treat the cavity distortion that is contributing to both the bleeding and the difficulty conceiving (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Refer for hysteroscopic resection of the submucosal fibroid
options.rationale: A submucosal fibroid with less than half its volume in the myometrium is amenable to hysteroscopic resection, which reduces menstrual loss and improves conception rates in a woman trying to become pregnant (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding; RANZCOG Fibroids).

options.text: Refer for total abdominal hysterectomy and ovarian conservation
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is definitive for bleeding but ends fertility, which is unacceptable to a woman actively trying to conceive with an otherwise treatable single lesion (Source: RANZCOG Heavy Menstrual Bleeding).

explanation.summary: Treatment of fibroid related heavy menstrual bleeding is decided by location far more than by size, which is why the FIGO classification numbers fibroids from 0 for wholly intracavitary through to 7 for pedunculated subserosal. Types 0, 1 and 2 are submucosal and are the ones most strongly associated with both heavy bleeding and impaired implantation, and types 0 and 1 are the ones removable hysteroscopically because less than half their volume sits in the myometrium. The presence of a reproductive intention changes the whole algorithm, ruling out hysterectomy, endometrial ablation and embolisation. The iron deficiency should be treated in parallel, since a ferritin of 8 micrograms per litre with microcytic anaemia will not correct without replacement even after the bleeding is controlled.
key_points: Fibroid location determines treatment more than fibroid size
FIGO types 0 and 1 are amenable to hysteroscopic resection
Submucosal fibroids impair implantation as well as causing heavy bleeding
Reproductive intention excludes ablation, embolisation and hysterectomy
Treat the iron deficiency in parallel with the structural problem
explanation.pearls: A FIGO type 2 fibroid has more than half its volume within the myometrium and is usually beyond safe hysteroscopic resection, so the proportion inside the cavity rather than the diameter decides whether a hysteroscopic approach is possible.

subtopic_detail: Fluid and vitamin choices when rehydrating a woman with prolonged pregnancy vomiting
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 26 year old woman at nine weeks in her first pregnancy who has vomited eight to ten times a day for two weeks and has kept nothing down for the past 48 hours. Her booking weight two weeks ago was 68 kg and she now weighs 63 kg.

She is not febrile, has no abdominal pain, no diarrhoea and no urinary symptoms. Her mucous membranes are dry and her skin turgor is reduced. Ultrasound today shows a single viable intrauterine pregnancy with no molar features, and she has taken no antiemetic other than ginger tablets.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 133 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), bicarbonate 20 mmol/L (22-32), creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), urinalysis ketones 3 plus
data_table.Additional tests: Thyroid stimulating hormone 0.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0) with free thyroxine at the upper limit of normal and no goitre or eye signs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous 5 per cent glucose with intravenous metoclopramide
options.rationale: Glucose containing fluid given before thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in a woman with prolonged vomiting, and dextrose alone does not replace the sodium and potassium she has lost (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy

options.text: Prescribe oral pyridoxine with doxylamine and review her in 48 hours
options.rationale: Oral first line antiemetics are appropriate for milder disease, but a woman who has kept nothing down for 48 hours will not absorb them and needs parenteral treatment (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy

options.text: Prescribe oral ondansetron and arrange community midwife review
options.rationale: The same absorption problem applies, and this plan leaves a dehydrated hypokalaemic woman with a 7 per cent weight loss to manage at home (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy

options.text: Admit for enteral feeding through a fine bore nasogastric tube
options.rationale: Enteral feeding is considered only after intravenous rehydration and combination antiemetics have failed over several days, so it is not the initial step (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy

options.text: Admit for intravenous sodium chloride with intravenous thiamine
options.rationale: Isotonic saline with added potassium corrects the volume and electrolyte deficit, and thiamine is given before or with any carbohydrate load because vomiting beyond three weeks depletes stores and risks Wernicke encephalopathy (Source: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum is defined by protracted vomiting with dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and weight loss of more than 5 per cent of booking weight, and it is distinguished from ordinary nausea and vomiting of pregnancy by those objective features rather than by symptom severity alone. Isotonic saline with potassium is the fluid of choice because these women are sodium and potassium depleted, while dextrose containing fluid can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in a thiamine deplete patient and offers no advantage. A suppressed thyroid stimulating hormone with a high normal free thyroxine and no goitre or eye signs is gestational transient thyrotoxicosis driven by human chorionic gonadotrophin, which resolves as the pregnancy advances and does not need antithyroid treatment. Antiemetics are then given parenterally in a stepwise fashion, and thromboprophylaxis is considered because dehydration and immobility raise thrombotic risk.
key_points: Weight loss above 5 per cent with ketosis and electrolyte disturbance defines the condition
Isotonic saline with potassium is the fluid of choice, not dextrose
Give thiamine before or with any carbohydrate containing fluid
Transient gestational thyrotoxicosis needs no antithyroid treatment
Consider thromboprophylaxis during admission for dehydration
explanation.pearls: Thiamine 100 mg intravenously daily for three days is given to any pregnant woman who has vomited for more than three weeks before glucose containing fluid is started, because Wernicke encephalopathy in this setting typically presents with confusion and eye signs after rehydration rather than before it.

sources.label: RANZCOG Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy
